strengths: MG-Select is a simple and practically appealing way to rank sampled VLA actions using only signals from the policy itself, avoiding a separately trained verifier.
The empirical scope is broader than many robotics papers: three simulation benchmarks, two autoregressive VLA architectures, low-data settings, and real-robot experiments.

The paper includes useful ablations of candidate count, masking choice, reference-distribution temperature, token aggregation, and joint training, as well as a single-prefill implementation that substantially reduces sampling overhead.

Some improvements are meaningful, particularly on low-data RoboCasa pick-and-place tasks and the reported real-world tasks, suggesting that condition-masked distributions may contain useful selection signals.
The presentation is generally clear, and the main algorithm is straightforward to implement for autoregressive policies.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol has a serious model-selection concern: the authors search over sampling temperature, candidate count, masking variant, reference temperature, and aggregation strategy, then report the best configuration for each dataset or policy without identifying a held-out validation set. Selecting among this large space on benchmark test performance could substantially inflate the reported gains.

The central interpretation is insufficiently justified. Masking conditions does not guarantee a maximally uncertain reference distribution—the paper itself observes that it can be sharply peaked—and maximizing reverse KL, KL(Q||P), is not established as a measure of candidate correctness or calibrated confidence. The strongest settings depend on empirical temperature smoothing and an ad hoc first-five-token aggregation rule.

The claimed benefit of verifier-free test-time selection is frequently conflated with the effect of changing training. The main SIMPLER, LIBERO, and in-distribution real-robot results use MG-Select*, which includes joint training. On the reported RoboCasa ablation, joint training alone produces most of the pick-and-place gain (17.0 to 28.5), while selection adds a smaller increase (28.5 to 31.0). Equivalent joint-training-only controls are missing on the other benchmarks.

Evidence is not consistently strong: LIBERO average improvements are only 1.6 and 1.1 percentage points and include regressions on several suites; SIMPLER improves by only 3.4 points; and the 300-demonstration RoboCasa result is nearly unchanged. Thus, claims of consistent and general improvement are stronger than the results support.

The real-robot evaluation uses only 16 or 24 trials per reported task aggregate and provides no confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or repeated-training seeds. With these sample sizes, several apparent gains may have substantial statistical uncertainty.

Baseline comparisons are incomplete. Published results from other models are not controlled for training data or compute, and the paper does not directly compare against external-verifier methods under matched models, candidate budgets, and latency. This limits support for claims that the proposed framework is preferable to existing test-time scaling approaches.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the exact selected hyperparameters for each reported benchmark are not given, the validation and checkpoint-selection protocols are unclear, and the manually collected real-world dataset and detailed evaluation protocol are not described sufficiently. The joint-training equation also suggests uniform averaging over four masking cases, whereas the implementation uses 10%/10%/10% dropout and therefore a different weighting.

The efficient deployment result reduces overhead but does not make scaling free: at N=16 the reported latency is 30.4 seconds versus 20.2 at N=1. The latency metric is also described ambiguously as inference latency averaged over episodes, without hardware, batch-memory usage, or control-frequency details.

Verifier-free candidate selection is practically relevant, simple to integrate with autoregressive VLAs, and avoids training a separate value model.
The evaluation spans RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, and a real Franka robot, and includes two VLA architectures.
The RoboCasa study examines candidate count, masking variants, temperature, score aggregation, joint training, and latency.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol has a major model-selection problem: the authors search sampling temperature, candidate count, masking variant, and reference temperature separately for each dataset and report the best result, but specify no held-out validation sets. Aggregation rules also appear empirically selected. Tuning this large configuration space on evaluation performance can readily produce optimistic gains, especially where improvements are only 1–3 percentage points.

The headline results frequently conflate MG-Select with an additional joint-training intervention. SIMPLER, LIBERO, and the real-world ID experiment report only MG-Select*, without joint-training-only or untrained-MG-Select controls. On RoboCasa, joint training alone explains a substantial fraction of the improvement. This weakens both the attribution to test-time selection and the prominent claim that the approach requires no additional training.

Statistical evidence is inadequate. Although simulation results are said to average three seeds, no standard deviations, confidence intervals, seed-level values, or significance tests are reported. The real-world studies use only 24 trials per ID task and 16 per OOD task; uncertainty is omitted despite large binomial variance. Relative improvements such as 168% further exaggerate changes from very low baselines.

The proposed score lacks convincing technical justification. Masking conditions does not guarantee a maximally uncertain distribution, and high KL divergence can indicate sensitivity or pathological overconfidence rather than action correctness. Moreover, the score compares complete next-token distributions and only depends on a sampled candidate through its prefix; the first-token score is identical for every candidate. No calibration, success-prediction, ranking-accuracy, or failure-case analysis establishes that this quantity is a reliable verifier.

Comparisons are insufficient for the central test-time-scaling claim. There is no matched evaluation against external-verifier methods such as value-guided sampling or RoboMonkey, and likelihood/uniform-KL alternatives are tested only in one RoboCasa configuration. Several other baselines are copied from prior papers under potentially different protocols.

The claimed generality is overstated. Much of the evidence concerns pick-and-place tasks, while LIBERO improvements are small on average and performance decreases on multiple suites. The method also requires dataset-specific choices of masking scheme and other hyperparameters rather than demonstrating a robust default configuration.

Reproducibility and efficiency reporting are incomplete: the selected hyperparameters for each policy/dataset are not disclosed, the single-prefill algorithm is not described sufficiently to reproduce, no code or trained-model release is stated, and latency is reported as episode-level time without hardware, action frequency, or a full accounting of the extra masked-distribution computation.

strengths: MG-Select offers a simple and practically relevant verifier-free approach to test-time scaling for autoregressive vision-language-action models, using the model’s condition-masked distributions rather than a separately trained value model.
The empirical study is unusually broad: it covers RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, and real-robot experiments, and includes both π0-FAST and OpenVLA backbones.
The paper includes useful component analyses of candidate count, masking variant, joint training, reference-distribution temperature, aggregation strategy, and inference latency.

Results are generally consistent with the proposed method helping difficult manipulation settings, with especially notable gains in low-data RoboCasa experiments and positive results on unseen real-world objects.
The single-prefill implementation substantially reduces the additional latency of Best-of-N sampling, improving the method’s practical relevance.
The manuscript is clear, well organized, and visually polished.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol creates a substantial model-selection concern: the authors search over sampling temperature, candidate count, masking variant, and seven reference temperatures separately for each dataset and report the best result, without specifying a held-out validation set. Selecting configurations using test success rates could inflate the reported gains, several of which are small.

The strongest headline result—168% relative improvement on low-data RoboCasa—combines MG-Select with joint training and starts from a very low success rate (5.3% to 14.2%). MG-Select alone reaches 7.2%, so this headline overstates the contribution of test-time selection itself.

Real-robot evidence is encouraging but statistically limited. The OOD results use only two tasks with 16 trials per task, and the ID results use 24 trials per task. No confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or repeated training seeds are provided, making it unclear whether several gains are robust.

The paper provides no theoretical or calibration evidence that KL(Q||P) is a valid confidence measure for action quality. Masking conditions does not necessarily produce maximum uncertainty, and maximizing divergence from the masked distribution could reward condition sensitivity rather than correct actions.

Some design choices are strongly benchmark-dependent and empirically selected, including which modality to mask and whether to aggregate only the first five tokens. This weakens the claim of a broadly applicable, plug-and-play selection rule.

The overall gains on stronger benchmarks are modest and mixed: LIBERO average improvements are only 1.1–1.6 points, with regressions on some suites, while SIMPLER improves by 3.4 points. Variance estimates are absent, so the significance of these differences is uncertain.

The claim of requiring no additional training needs qualification: the basic method is training-free, but many principal results, including all LIBERO, SIMPLER, and real-world ID comparisons, use the proposed joint-training procedure.

Reproducibility is incomplete: implementation details are provided, but there is no code or checkpoint release statement, the real-world dataset is not described as available, and evaluation details such as trial randomization, failure criteria, uncertainty estimates, and hyperparameter-selection splits are missing.

This large search space, together with dataset-specific aggregation choices, can substantially inflate results and undermines the central empirical claim.

Most headline results use MG-Select*, which includes additional joint training. This weakens the verifier-free/no-additional-training framing and confounds gains from test-time selection with gains from condition-dropout regularization. MG-Select without retraining is not reported across most benchmarks.

No standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests are provided. This is especially problematic because several gains are only 1–3 percentage points, performance sometimes decreases on individual LIBERO suites, and the real-world studies use only 16 or 24 trials per task, yielding considerable statistical uncertainty.

Baseline comparisons are not consistently controlled. Several numbers come from prior papers with potentially different training setups, while the RoboMonkey comparison removes Gaussian perturbation and majority voting rather than evaluating the complete published method. Thus, claims of competitiveness with external verifiers are not firmly established.

The technical novelty is moderate: the method adapts Best-of-N/self-certainty ideas by replacing a uniform reference with a condition-masked model distribution. The entropy theorem is elementary and only shows that temperature increases entropy; it does not justify why maximizing KL from the masked distribution should correlate with action correctness.

The method requires substantial task-dependent tuning and can hurt already strong policies, limiting the claim that it consistently improves VLAs. Overall, the work is promising and technically plausible, but the evaluation protocol needs stronger controls before it is competitive for acceptance.

strengths: The paper presents a simple, clearly described verifier-free Best-of-N method that can be applied to autoregressive VLAs without adding an external reward or value model.

The component studies examine candidate count, masking variants, dropout ratios, temperature, token aggregation, and latency. The single-prefill implementation substantially reduces the overhead of parallel candidate generation.
The reported results are generally directionally consistent, with improvements concentrated on difficult tasks and weaker base policies.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol risks substantial test-set overfitting. The authors search sampling temperature, candidate count, masking type, and reference temperature separately for every dataset and policy, then report the best result, but specify no held-out validation set or selection criterion. This search covers up to roughly 210 configurations before considering aggregation choices. Some reported gains are small enough to be readily explained by such selection.

The main contribution is confounded with joint training. On the central RoboCasa ablation, joint training alone raises pick-and-place success from 17.0 to 28.5, whereas MG-Select adds only 2.5 points to the jointly trained model. Nevertheless, most headline comparisons on SIMPLER, LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-world ID tasks compare MG-Select with joint training against a vanilla-trained base model, without reporting the corresponding joint-training-only control. The evidence therefore does not establish that the proposed test-time selector causes most of the gains.

The proposed score lacks a convincing technical justification. KL(Q||P) measures disagreement between entire next-token distributions and does not directly score the candidate token itself; at the first token it is identical for every candidate. Maximizing reverse KL can also reward an incorrectly overconfident conditional distribution. The entropy theorem only proves the elementary fact that softmax entropy increases with temperature and provides no link between the score and action correctness.

The evidence that condition masking is better than simpler selection is weak. In the principal ablation, MG-Select improves over likelihood selection by only 0.5 points on pick-and-place and 1.3 points overall, with no confidence intervals or significance tests. After applying a high temperature to the masked reference, it also approaches the uniform-reference baseline conceptually, yet the paper does not quantify how much task-specific information remains.

The paper reports averages over seeds but not variances, confidence intervals, or paired tests. This is especially problematic for the real-robot results, which use only 16 or 24 trials per task and consequently have very coarse success-rate increments. The claimed 28% and 35% relative improvements sound large but may correspond to only a few additional successful trials.

Baseline comparisons are not consistently controlled. Several simulation baselines are copied from prior papers despite different models and training setups. The direct RoboMonkey comparison modifies that method by removing Gaussian perturbation and majority voting, so it does not evaluate the published system. Compute-matched comparisons against likelihood, uniform-KL, and external-verifier approaches across all major benchmarks are missing.

Novelty is limited: the method adapts existing self-certainty/Best-of-N ideas using condition dropout, while the strongest empirical ingredient resembles standard modality dropout regularization. The manuscript does not demonstrate that this combination yields a robust, generally applicable confidence estimator rather than a dataset-tuned heuristic.

The claims are stronger than the results. Performance decreases on several LIBERO suites, gains on strong π0-FAST are only 1.1 points on average, and the standalone training-free version is evaluated much less comprehensively than MG-Select*. Thus the broad claim of consistent improvement without additional training is not adequately supported.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the implementation appendix: no code or trained checkpoints are provided, the real-world dataset and evaluation randomization are unspecified, and the precise protocol used to select deployment hyperparameters is absent. Overall, the promising empirical idea is not supported rigorously enough for acceptance at a top-tier venue.

strengths: MG-Select offers a simple, practically relevant approach to test-time scaling for autoregressive vision-language-action models without requiring a separately trained verifier. Using condition-masked model distributions as internal reference signals is intuitive and potentially useful.
The empirical study is unusually broad: it covers RoboCasa, SIMPLER-WidowX, LIBERO, CALVIN, and real-robot experiments, with multiple VLA architectures and model scales.
The paper includes useful component ablations covering candidate count, masking variants, joint training, reference temperature, aggregation strategy, and dropout ratio.
The authors examine deployment cost and propose a single-prefill implementation that substantially reduces the latency overhead of sampling multiple candidates.
The presentation is clear and well organized, and the strongest results—particularly in low-data RoboCasa settings and the real-world evaluations—are encouraging.
weaknesses: The hyperparameter-selection protocol is a major concern. The authors search over sampling temperature, candidate count, masking type, reference temperature, and aggregation behavior for each dataset or policy and report the best result, but do not specify a separate validation set. If benchmark test performance guided these choices, the comparisons are optimistically biased and do not establish a deployable selection rule for unseen tasks.

There is an apparent technical inconsistency in the aggregation experiments. Under the stated autoregressive definition, the KL score for the first token is conditioned on the same observation and empty prefix for every candidate, so it must be identical across candidates. Nevertheless, Tables 5 and 12 report distinct Best-of-N behavior for “First 1,” including substantial improvements. This requires clarification and raises concerns about whether the implementation matches the equations.

The largest gains generally come from MG-Select*, which changes training through condition dropout. Thus, the evidence for the advertised training-free applicability is materially weaker: plain MG-Select is not reported on several principal benchmarks, while joint training alone already produces large gains on RoboCasa.

The mathematical training objective appears to average uniformly over four masking configurations, whereas the implementation uses 10%/10%/10% dropout and therefore approximately 70% unmasked examples. This mismatch impairs technical clarity and reproducibility.

The paper searches many configurations but reports no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests. Several headline gains are small—for example, 92.0 to 93.1 on LIBERO—and the real-world OOD evaluation has only 16 trials per task, making the reliability of the reported relative improvements difficult to assess.

The external-verifier comparison is limited to one benchmark and modifies RoboMonkey by removing parts of its procedure. MG-Select is only approximately tied there (50.3 versus 50.7), so the broader claim of replacing external verification is not yet convincingly established.

The central rationale—that a larger reverse KL divergence from a masked distribution identifies a better action—is heuristic. The entropy theorem only shows that temperature increases reference entropy; it does not justify the ranking criterion or demonstrate that the score is calibrated with action success.

Reproducibility remains incomplete: the selected deployment hyperparameters for each benchmark are not enumerated, the validation procedure is absent, and no code or release commitment is provided. Overall, the contribution is promising, but these evaluation and consistency issues place it slightly below the acceptance threshold.
